newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower in pre-holiday trade.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower in pre-holiday trade.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended a holiday-shortened session lower Friday, on fund selling after a breach of support levels, despite a slump in U.S. treasury bond and equity markets.
U.S. markets are closed Monday for the Labor Day holiday.

"It's a bit discouraging that precious metals got no support from the nervousness in debt and equity markets, but Japanese disinvestment looks to be continuing, with this week's quarterly Tankan report showing the Japanese economy still struggling to get out of recession," Refco's New York analyst James Steel said.
COMEX December gold ended down $1.10 an ounce at $391.30, after recovering late from a session low at $390.00, the contract's lowest level for nearly a month.

In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $386.50/387.00, after seeing a session low around $385.60, compared to the London afternoon fix Friday $386.45 and the close in New York Thursday at $387.60/388.00.

A New York Times report Friday, describing a revised IMF debt relief plan for poor countries, which involves selling some IMF gold, had little impact as the plan had been discussed for some months, traders said.

The IMF debt relief plan, first discussed by the Group of Seven (G-7) leading industrial countries in 1995, would involve the sale over time of about five million ounces, or five percent, of the IMF's 104 million ounce gold reserve.
COMEX silver ended down 0.5 cents at $5.250, after seeing a session low at $5.180.
"The rally in silver looks to be failing also, with a drift back down to support around $5.100 basis December now possible," one trader said.
NYMEX October platinum ended down $1.70 an ounce at $398.90, after seeing a fresh four week low at $397.10.
NYMEX December palladium ended off $1.00 an ounce at $126.50.
"The fact that dealers have been able to push platinum to $400 once again, and break below this level, means this metal is vulnerable to further selling," one analyst said.
